name: Fit for Life diet

card.summary: A 1980s food-combining eating plan (fruit in the morning, no protein-carbohydrate pairing) that followers adopt to lose weight and improve skin, energy and overall look.
card.note: Listed as a fad diet by professional nutrition bodies.

quick.overview:
Fit for Life is a diet-and-lifestyle programme popularised by Harvey and Marilyn Diamond from 1985. Its rules centre on eating fruit alone in the morning, not combining protein and starch in one meal, and limiting dairy. Followers adopt it mainly for weight loss and a leaner look, and some for skin and energy.

The approach draws on Herbert Shelton's food-combining ideas. Professional bodies classify it as a fad diet, while the authors report millions of copies sold.
quick.how: People follow the combining rules: fruit in the morning, protein and carbohydrate foods at separate meals, water apart from meals, and little dairy. Later editions added personalised and supplement elements.
quick.risks: Nutrition organisations including the American Dietetic Association list it as a fad diet, and critics question the credentials and scientific basis of its claims. Restrictive combining rules may make meal planning harder for some people.

lead: Fit for Life is a diet and lifestyle book series by Harvey and Marilyn Diamond, first published in the United States in 1985. The programme rests on 'natural hygiene' ideas from Herbert Shelton and sorts foods into those that supposedly 'clog' the body and those that 'cleanse' it [1].

People use it chiefly to lose weight and look and feel leaner. Its main rules are to eat fresh fruit alone, ideally in the morning, to avoid mixing carbohydrates and proteins in one meal, to avoid drinking water with meals and to eat little or no dairy [1].

The book was a New York Times best seller in the mid-1980s, and Harvey Diamond says it sold over 12 million copies. The American Dietetic Association and the American Academy of Family Physicians list it as a fad diet [1]. A 1987 dietetics report reviewed it alongside four other popular low-calorie diets [2].

chain: Follow fruit-first mornings and no protein-carb pairing
Calorie intake and food choices change
Weight loss and, per followers, clearer skin and more energy
angle.text: Followers use the plan to lose weight and look leaner, and some report clearer skin and more energy. Any weight change is through altered eating patterns rather than the combining rules specifically.

infobox: Fruit alone in the morning; no protein-carb meals

paras: The programme divides foods into 'living' and 'dead' foods, and its principal rules are fruit alone in the morning, no combining carbohydrates with proteins, water apart from meals and minimal dairy [1].

The first book appeared in 1985 and Fit for Life II followed in 1989. Later titles include Fit for Life: A New Beginning (2001), Fit for Life Not Fat For Life (2003) and Living Without Pain (2007). In the 2000s the Diamonds added a personalised approach using metabolic typing and began selling enzyme supplements. Tony Robbins promoted the principles in his book Unlimited Power [1].

The American Dietetic Association and the American Academy of Family Physicians list Fit for Life as a fad diet, and critics say many of its claimed benefits lack scholarly citations. Harvey Diamond's doctorate came from a non-accredited correspondence school, which critics have raised in questioning his nutrition expertise [1]. A 2000 study cited in the Wikipedia article reported that a dissociated diet works about as well for weight loss as a calorie-restricted diet [1].

No studies found on Fit for Life as a programme. A 1987 technical report in Topics in Clinical Nutrition reviewed it with the Cambridge diet, the protein-sparing modified fast, Weight Watchers and the Bloomingdale Eat Healthy Diet [2].
